intro: Booking a room, checking in, reporting a problem, getting through the airport and finding your train: when you travel, the same situations and phrases come back again and again. This lesson gives you the polite phrases (Could I…?, I’d like…, lessons 34 and 57) and the key vocabulary, with the differences between British and American English.
objectifs: Book a room and say the type of room, the dates and what is included.
Check in and check out of a hotel, asking the right questions.
Report a problem in your room politely.
Manage at the airport and the station: check-in, luggage, boarding, delays.

texte: To book: “I’d like to book a room for two nights, from the 12th to the 14th of May.” Say the type of room: “a single room” (for one person), “a double room” (one big bed for two), “a twin room” (two separate beds), “a family room”.
Useful questions: “How much is it per night?”, “Is breakfast included?”, “Is there Wi-Fi in the room?”, “Have you got any rooms available?” (= free rooms).
Careful: a “twin room” has two separate beds. If you want one big bed, ask for “a double room”.

lignes: a room + breakfast, often in a small house

exemples: I’d like to book a double room for three nights, please.
Booking: type of room + number of nights.
How much is it per night, with breakfast?
Asking the price.
Have you got any rooms available for tonight?
available = free, not booked.

sections.titre: Arriving and leaving: check in, check out
texte: At reception: “Hello, I’ve got a reservation. The name’s Kamga.” or “I’d like to check in, please.” The receptionist often asks: “Can I see your passport, please?” and gives you “your key card” and your room number.
Questions to ask: “What time is breakfast?”, “What time is check-out?” (= when must you leave the room?), “Can I leave my luggage here?”
“check in” and “check out” are phrasal verbs (lesson 72): “We checked in at three.” The nouns have a hyphen: “Check-in is from 2 p.m.”
exemples: I’d like to check in, please. I’ve got a reservation under the name Nkomo.
Arriving at the hotel.
What time is check-out? — Eleven o’clock.
check-out (noun) = the time you must leave.
Could I have a wake-up call at six, please?
The hotel phones you to wake you up.

texte: Start politely: “Excuse me, I’m sorry to bother you, but…” or “I’m afraid there’s a problem with my room.” (“I’m afraid” here means “I’m sorry to say”.)
Common problems: “The air conditioning doesn’t work.” / “The shower isn’t working.”, “There are no towels.”, “The room is very noisy.”, “The room hasn’t been cleaned.”
To ask for a solution: “Could someone come and look at it?”, “Could I change rooms, please?” Careful: “change rooms”, with an s.
exemples: I’m afraid the heating doesn’t work in room 214.
I’m afraid = a polite way to start bad news.
Excuse me, there’s no hot water. Could someone come and look at it?
Problem + polite request.
The room is very noisy. Could I change rooms, please?
change rooms (plural).

texte: The steps: “check in” at the desk or online, “drop off your bags”, “go through security”, “go to the gate”, “board the plane”.

Vocabulary: “a boarding pass” (the card you need to get on the plane), “hand luggage” (bags you take on the plane; US “carry-on”), “checked luggage” (bags that travel under the plane), “a delay”, “The flight is delayed / cancelled” (US “canceled”).
Careful: “luggage” and “baggage” are uncountable (lesson 59): don’t say “two luggages”; say “two bags” or “two pieces of luggage”.
exemples: Can I see your passport and boarding pass, please?
At check-in or at the gate.
I’ve got one suitcase and one piece of hand luggage.
a piece of + uncountable noun.
Our flight to Montreal is delayed by two hours.
be delayed by + time.
Boarding is at gate 32.
The gate = where you get on the plane.

sections.titre: At the station and on public transport
texte: Buying a ticket: “A single to Manchester, please.” (one way only; US “one-way”) / “A return to Oxford, please.” (there and back; US “round-trip”).
Asking for information: “Which platform does the train to York leave from?”, “What time is the next train to London?”, “Do I need to change?” (= take another train).
Asking the way quickly: “Excuse me, how do I get to the city centre?” / “Is it far from here?”
exemples: A return ticket to Brighton, please. — That’s £24.50.
Buying a train ticket (UK).
Which platform does the next train to Leeds leave from? — Platform 4.
platform = where you get on the train.
Excuse me, how do I get to the station from here?
Asking the way.
sections.note: “Travel” is mostly a verb or an uncountable noun (“I love travel”). For one particular journey, say “a trip” or “a journey”: “Have a good trip!”

formule: I’d like to book a double room for two nights. · I’d like to check in / check out, please. · I’m afraid the shower doesn’t work. · A return to…, please. · My flight is delayed.
prononciation: “hotel” /həʊˈtel/: stress on the second syllable, “ho-TEL”, and say the h.
“queue” (a line of people waiting) is /kjuː/, like the letter Q.
erreurs: I'd like to reserve a chamber.
I'd like to book a room.
A hotel room is “a room”; “book” is more common than “reserve”.
I have two bags. / I have two pieces of luggage.
The shower doesn't work. / The shower isn't working.
Our flight has a delay of two hours.
Our flight is delayed by two hours. / Our flight is two hours late.
I'd like a return-trip for Oxford.
a return (UK) / a round-trip ticket (US); destination with “to”.
Have a good trip! / Have a safe journey!

dialogue.contexte: Amina, from Yaoundé, arrives at a hotel in London in the evening after a delayed flight.
lignes: Good evening. How can I help you?
Hello. I’d like to check in, please. I’ve got a reservation under the name Abena.
Yes, a single room for three nights. Can I see your passport, please?
Here you are. Sorry I’m late, my flight was delayed.
Here you are = when you give something.
No problem. Here’s your key card. You’re in room 308, on the third floor.
Thank you. Is breakfast included? And what time is it?
Yes, it is. It’s from seven to ten in the restaurant.
(Later, on the phone) Hello, I’m afraid the air conditioning doesn’t work in room 308.
I’m so sorry. I’ll send someone up right away.
send someone up = send a person to the room.

mots: book
I booked a twin room online.
ask for a room, seat or table for a later time
check in
You can check in from 2 p.m.
arrive and register at a hotel or airport
check out
We have to check out before eleven.
pay and leave a hotel
available
Have you got any rooms available?
free, that you can have or use
luggage
Can I leave my luggage at reception?
the bags you travel with (uncountable)
boarding pass
Keep your boarding pass with your passport.
the card you need to get on a plane
delayed
The train is delayed by twenty minutes.
later than planned
platform
The train leaves from platform 6.
the place in a station where you get on a train
return ticket
A return ticket is cheaper than two singles.
a ticket to go somewhere and come back (UK)
trip
Have a good trip!
a journey to a place and back

exercices.consigne: Give the type of room: single, double or twin.
items: A couple who want one big bed.
Two colleagues who each want their own bed.
Two friends who don’t want to share a bed.
I’d like to ___ in, please. I’ve got a reservation.
The flight to Douala is ___ by an hour.
Which ___ does the train to Bath leave from?
Can I see your passport and ___ pass, please?

exercices.consigne: Write a polite sentence to report the problem and ask for a solution.
items: I’m afraid the shower doesn’t work. Could someone come and look at it?
Excuse me, there are no towels in my room. Could I have some, please?
I’m sorry, but my room is very noisy. Could I change rooms, please?
Excuse me, the Wi-Fi isn’t working in my room. Could you help me?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I’ve got two bags. / I’ve got two pieces of luggage.
A return to Cambridge, please. (US: a round-trip ticket)
What time is the check-out of the room?
Have you got any rooms disponible tonight?
Have you got any rooms available tonight?

exercices.consigne: Write a short dialogue (6 to 8 lines): you arrive at a hotel, check in, ask two questions, then report a problem.
items: Receptionist: Good afternoon. Can I help you? Me: Yes, I’d like to check in, please. I’ve got a reservation under the name Fotso. Receptionist: A double room for two nights. Can I see your passport? Me: Here you are. What time is breakfast? Receptionist: From seven to half past nine. Me: And can I leave my luggage here tomorrow after check-out? Receptionist: Of course. (Later) Me: Hello, I’m afraid there’s no hot water in room 112. Could someone come and look at it? Receptionist: I’m so sorry, I’ll send someone right away.

a_retenir: Book: I’d like to book a single / double / twin room for two nights. Twin = two separate beds.
At the hotel: check in (arrive), check out (leave); Is breakfast included? What time is check-out?
Problem: I’m afraid the… doesn’t work. Could someone come and look at it? Could I change rooms?
Airport: boarding pass, hand luggage, gate, delayed, cancelled. “luggage” is uncountable.
Station: a single / a return to…; Which platform…? Have a good trip!
